item.title: Looking Back on the Summer of High MAGA in Trump's Washington
item.description:
When the history of this time is written, it may be observed that the United States of America celebrated its 250th anniversary with one, big Donald Trump-themed party in the nation’s capital that lasted for one whole summer.

That is how it has looked, at times, over these last few months in Washington, where Mr. Trump used the occasion of the nation’s birthday to throw a series of parties done up in the distinct and florid style of the political movement he created, even as his presidency faced new perils.

It was an absolute MAGA-extravaganza, all summer long, and the imagery was something to behold.

There was an IndyCar race around the National Mall and an eight-sided fighting cage wrapped in crypto advertisements on the south lawn of the White House. Remember “the Claw,” how it towered like a jumbo inflatable bouncy house beside the White House?

On July 4, Mr. Trump stood before the Washington Monument during a lightning storm and ministered to his most faithful followers while surrounded by tattered American flags from key moments throughout the nation’s history.

The monuments and landmarks of the city changed. The reflecting pool turned green. The Kennedy Center shut down. National Guard troops patrolling the city posted up by great old fountains that were shooting water again for the first time in a long time.

Much of what was staged in Washington these last few months was done so under the banner of the nation’s 250th anniversary — but it was the nation’s 250th anniversary as directed by Mr. Trump.

Disparate elements of his base converged on the capital, rendering a portrait of his movement.

In May, families prayed on the national mall at “a celebration of America’s Christian history.” Billionaires with business before the Trump administration sat ringside at the White House UFC fight that the president threw on his 80th birthday. Young men watching the fight from the overflow area on the Ellipse roared at the spectacle of it.

A man with a Three Percenters tattoo took pictures of a military flyover during the IndyCar race. The pious, the ultrawealthy, the hypermasculine, the extremist — all made pilgrimages to the capital for this high-MAGA summer.

But the summer is ending. Mr. Trump’s approval ratings hit a new low in August. High-level White House staff have started to exit. An increasing number of his supporters with big social media followings are defecting.

There is no getting around the fact that Mr. Trump is a lame-duck president. As one of his favorite historical figures, Winston Churchill, famously said: “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.”

How did Mr. Trump and his MAGA movement express themselves at their maximal moment?

Like this.

item.title: Trump Officials Draft Plan to Pay At-Home Parents, Using Funds for Working Ones
item.description:
The Trump administration is moving to allow married couples with a stay-at-home spouse to collect child care subsidies, a policy championed by Vice President JD Vance, using funds from a federal program intended to assist working parents, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The change would create the only federal subsidy to pay parents to stay home and raise their children, one of the most significant efforts to date by the Trump administration to harness federal funds to promote a traditional view of families.

To do so, officials are seeking to use a Health and Human Services Department fund that was created in the 1990s to help low-income and working-class parents afford child care so they could work or go to school.

Under the draft new rule, parents who stay home with their children could benefit from the program, which typically provides about $9,000 per child each year, potentially reshaping which families get federal child care money.

The move could end up redirecting money away from working parents and their child care providers, causing some to raise their rates or even close, critics said, potentially worsening what many experts say is a child care crisis in the country.

About 80 percent of the 870,000 families who currently get the child care subsidies have single working parents, most of them mothers, according to Health Department data.

The policy change would effectively create a government incentive for parents to stay home with their children, an idea embraced as part of a broader conservative effort to advance policies that promote more mothers staying at home.

The new rule being drafted would allow married couples with one stay-at-home parent in certain income brackets to collect a subsidy, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the plan before it is finalized. The change could be made without approval from Congress.

More than 80 percent of stay-at-home parents are mothers, according to the Pew Research Center.

The plan is being pushed by the White House and is seen as a top priority of Mr. Vance, according to several people familiar with the discussions. The draft rule also incorporates policies in legislation written by Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he was a senator from Florida.

Representatives for the White House, Mr. Vance and the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Vance, whose wife Usha, a former corporate lawyer, gave birth to their fourth child in July, has long advocated for more mothers to stay at home with young children and called for efforts to open up child care subsidy programs to those providing “kinship care.”

In 2021, Mr. Vance co-wrote an opinion essay in The Wall Street Journal contending that day care can harm children and declaring, “Young children are clearly happier and healthier when they spend the day at home with a parent.”

He also wrote then on Twitter that “normal Americans” want a “family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap day care so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force.”

Some family policy experts said the changes to the program would hurt parents who have to work and have difficulty affording child care.

“I am a big proponent of more support for stay-at-home parents. But this is not how I would choose to do it,” said Patrick T. Brown, a fellow at the Life and Family Initiative at the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank.

“Expanding the eligibility without increasing funding would mean more parents competing for the same dollars, and leaving more parents — particularly single working parents — worse off,” he said.

The $12 billion Child Care and Development Fund, which is run by the Health Department’s Administration for Children and Families, was created during the Clinton administration to support the employment of low to moderate-income parents. It subsidizes the care of children up to age 13 and currently offsets the costs for caring for about 1.3 million children.

Under the current rules, most of the money is distributed to states, which in turn distribute it to parents, usually in the form of vouchers or direct deposits to child care providers.

To qualify, parents must prove that their income is lower than 85 percent of their state’s median income and that they are working, in school or receiving job training. Some states set a lower threshold of 60 percent of the state’s median income.

Under the proposed rule changes, the same pot of money would also be used to pay married parents who meet the income requirements when one parent works and the other cares for the child. The money would be intended to help offset the lost income of the stay-at-home parent.

The proposal “creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C.C.D.F. assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week,” according to a draft document viewed by The Times.

Unmarried couples in which one parent stays at home would not qualify under the draft. Single parents who do not work are currently not eligible for the subsidy, nor would they be under the new proposal for married couples.

The rule, which could still be changed before publication, would need to be approved by the White House and then would be posted online for public comment. If it is finalized, it could go into effect as soon as next year.

Some department lawyers working on the plan have questioned the legality of requiring recipients to be married, according to the people familiar with the matter. Some have also raised concerns about whether the change could increase the risk of fraud, since the money would be going to individuals rather than businesses. The administration has sought to crack down on fraud in social services programs, particularly child care.

The idea of paying parents to stay home was outlined in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint published by the Heritage Foundation ahead of Mr. Trump’s return to office, much of which overlaps with the administration’s policy agenda.

“Instead of providing universal day care, funding should go to parents either to offset the cost of staying home with a child or to pay for familial, in-home child care,” it says, although it does not specify how or which fund to use.

“You don’t need statutes to do it, and with existing programs we can end discrimination against stay-at-home parents,” said Roger Severino, a vice president at the Heritage Foundation who wrote the Project 2025 section on child care policy.

“It would be a welcome change to see equal treatment between commercial day care and the contribution stay-at-home parents provide in caring for and raising the next generation,” he said in an interview. “It doesn’t get more pro-family than that.”

Mr. Severino said he believed that the provision privileging married parents would most likely withstand a legal challenge. He said that under the Supreme Court decision Obergefell v. Hodges, married same-sex parents would most likely also qualify for the subsidies.

In a letter to governors on Mother’s Day, Alex Adams, the head of the Administration for Children and Families, previewed that policy changes were coming and urged states to “use every available” flexibility to distribute federal money in ways that “support married two-parent families,” and particularly “families who choose to have a parent remain at home with young children.”

Child care policy experts said they anticipate that in some states, the rule change could lead to much of the money going to stay-at-home parents. States have some flexibility in determining how their subsidies from the Child Care and Development Fund are allocated, and lawmakers in some red states, including Idaho, Wyoming and Utah, have pushed for new policies for the states to support stay-at-home parents.

That outcome could in turn shutter some of the roughly 225,000 child care providers that rely on the subsidies for tuition payments.

Krystal Gastineau, the owner of Cribs 2 Crayons, a child-care center in Aurora, Colo., said that about half the children she cares for receive the subsidies, which are paid directly to Ms. Gastineau’s business via direct deposit. “If they could, I think parents would choose to take the money and stay home,” she said. “That would take away a major source of income.”

“I think that’s a misuse of the system,” she said.

Lezlie Cranston, in Auburn, Wash., uses the subsidy program to pay for care for her 4-year-old son, Ricky, and her 2-year-old daughter, Samantha, while she pursues a certification at Skagit Valley College. The subsidies have “helped tremendously with allowing me to do my coursework,” said Ms. Cranston, a single parent.

“But changing it to let the money go to stay-at-home parents is going to create conflict between parents,” she said. “That’s a bad situation. We’re already trying to figure out how more working parents can get the subsidies. This could lead to single parents not being able to afford child care again.”

item.title: Trump’s Super PAC Will Spend $10 Million on Texas Senate Race
item.description:
President Trump’s super PAC has begun spending money in the 2026 midterm general elections, answering the call from many Republicans who have been eager for the financial support.

MAGA Inc., the super PAC allied with the president, on Saturday disclosed a $10 million digital and television ad buy to boost Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, and attack his Democratic opponent, James Talarico. The spending puts an end to a standoff between MAGA Inc. and several other G.O.P. groups over who would help finance ads for Mr. Paxton.

The filing on Saturday is the first general election spending by the super PAC, which has amassed an extraordinary cash reserve of more than $400 million.

During a news conference on Friday, Mr. Trump said MAGA Inc. would probably spend $400 million to $500 million in the midterms. “I’m going to help a lot of the congressmen and senators,” he added.

The Texas race is among the most competitive in the country and will help determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.

And Texas, with its 18-plus television markets, is an especially expensive setting to run a statewide campaign. In the Republican primary and subsequent runoff, nearly $130 million was spent on advertising.

On Saturday, MAGA Inc. released an ad calling Mr. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, the better candidate on the issue of taxes.

Even as the president has supported Mr. Paxton’s campaign, he has also disparaged him. “You might not like the way he looks, you might not love his look, you might not love his television interviews, but he was the best attorney general in the country, perhaps,” Mr. Trump said at a Rose Garden event this week.

Mr. Paxton brushed off the criticism during a Fox News appearance. “Texas is a rather casual place in the summer and it’s hot,” he said. “We adjust. Wear cowboy boots, a blazer, and we’re good.”

Mr. Paxton’s ability to raise money has been complicated by the grudges still held by some donors after a bruising Republican primary in which he beat the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn, with the help of an endorsement from Mr. Trump.

And Mr. Talarico, a state representative, has proved to be a prodigious fund-raiser.

item.title: A Hard Decision for the Hard-Nosed Prosecutor in Clancy Triple-Murder Case
item.description:
For his 25 years as the elected district attorney of Plymouth County, a working-class district between Boston and Cape Cod in Massachusetts, Timothy Cruz has honed his reputation as a hard-nosed prosecutor tough on crime.

With that in mind, colleagues and others who know his approach say they would be surprised if he backs off his prosecution of Lindsay Clancy, even after her case ended in a mistrial on Friday, with 11 of 12 jurors appearing to agree that she should not be found guilty of first-degree murder.

Encircled by a thicket of cameras and microphones after the trial, Mr. Cruz declined to immediately say if he planned to again try Ms. Clancy in the killing of her three children. But his tone and words did not suggest that he would soften his approach.

“This is, has been and will be about getting justice,” he said, invoking the memory of Ms. Clancy’s children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and baby Callan — and pledging to “make sure that the victims are not invisible.”

Mr. Cruz, the son of a plumber who was born in the blue-collar city of Brockton, said on Friday that he would make his decision about his next steps “shortly.”

Mr. Cruz has been sharply criticized by some supporters of Ms. Clancy for his decision to try her for first-degree murder instead of crafting an approach that acknowledged her mental illness and prioritized treatment over prison time. Ms. Clancy has admitted to strangling her children. Her lawyer argued that she was experiencing psychosis on Jan. 24, 2023, and heard a hallucinated male voice that ordered her to kill them.

During the trial that began in July, the assistant district attorneys Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham acknowledged Ms. Clancy’s struggles with depression and anxiety after the birth of her third child. But they also painted her as a manipulative and calculating killer who sent her husband out on errands to buy time to commit the murders, and then fabricated claims of psychosis to evade punishment after she survived her own suicide attempt.

“She no longer liked the life that she thought she wanted, and when she saw the opportunity to escape, she made the selfish choice to take it,” Ms. Buckingham said in her opening argument.

Robert F. Shaw, a Boston defense lawyer, said the prosecution’s approach was startling, given Ms. Clancy’s well-documented efforts before the killings to find effective treatment for her mental illness.

“If somebody’s struggling to get medical help and persistently seeking it out and obviously there’s been real impact on mental health, why frame it right from the start as this cold, calculating, manipulative woman?” Mr. Shaw said.

Experts said that most prosecutors would think twice about retrying a case after a hung jury in which they knew a large majority opposed a guilty finding, as seems to have been the case in Ms. Clancy’s mistrial. The expense of a second trial may be another deterrent. But in a case involving child victims that drew widespread national attention, an elected D.A. may feel heavy pressure to persist.

In Mr. Cruz’s case, a decision to retry Ms. Clancy on the same charge would also be in keeping with his uncompromising approach. Elliot Levine, a criminal defense lawyer, called Mr. Cruz’s office “the most draconian in the state.”

“He will try a case that is maybe a losing case,” Mr. Levine said. “That way it’s the jury’s fault but not his fault for being soft on crime.”

Mr. Cruz has been an outspoken critic of some recent criminal justice reforms in progressive Massachusetts, where he is the only Republican among the state’s 11 elected district attorneys. He is running unopposed for re-election in November.

Among his supporters in Plymouth County, including Hunter Young, chairman of the Plymouth Republican Town Committee, there is support for a retrial of Ms. Clancy.

“I think there was malice aforethought — that’s what the facts seem to show — and I think he should go for it again,” said Mr. Young, 21. “We want justice for the children. It’s not about her.”

Had Mr. Cruz opted for a second-degree murder charge against Ms. Clancy, her lawyer would have had the option to waive a jury trial and have the case heard by a judge alone. Some see that path as more humane for mentally ill defendants, or more just, given the complexity of insanity defenses.

Typically, Mr. Cruz has reserved his compassion for crime victims. He forcefully criticized a 2024 decision by the state’s Supreme Judicial Court that barred life sentences without parole for people who commit crimes before age 21, and decried as “travesties” the resulting release of some offenders by the state parole board.

“Massachusetts was once a national leader in protecting the rights of victims of crime,” he wrote in an editorial last year. “Sadly, those days are long gone.”

His leadership has come under fire before. He faced questions a decade ago about his slow response to sexual harassment allegations against his top deputy. He was criticized for spending more than $2 million on private lawyers to fight a wrongful termination lawsuit by a former prosecutor. And he was sued by the state’s attorney general for withholding public records.

In a recent setback for his office, Mr. Cruz was ordered by the state’s highest court to grant a new trial to Latarsha Sanders, another Massachusetts mother who killed her children while mentally ill, and was convicted of first-degree murder in 2022. The court found that her mental health records should not have been excluded from her trial by the judge; Mr. Cruz has not yet said if he intends to retry her.

A seasoned outsider in a state largely run by Democrats, Mr. Cruz can still bristle at criticism. Heckled by supporters of Ms. Clancy at his news conference on Friday, he snapped back. “I’m not going to stand out here and listen to this,” he said.

Asked to defend what some have called his insensitive treatment of Ms. Clancy, he wasted no time turning the tables. “Insensitive?” he shot back. “Insensitive is killing three children.”

A spokeswoman for Mr. Cruz’s office did not immediately grant an interview request.

Robert Bloom, a professor of law at Boston College — where Mr. Cruz earned his undergraduate degree and played hockey — said the prosecutor’s full-bore approach may reflect an insistence on evenhandedness. His district ranges from elite coastal enclaves like Duxbury, where the Clancys lived, to blue-collar cities like his native Brockton.

“In terms of working-class voters, you’ve got to say: We’re treating someone from Duxbury the same way we’re treating someone from Brockton,” said Professor Bloom.

Voters have responded, in a politically mixed county where President Trump won more than a dozen towns in the 2024 election. The last time Mr. Cruz was re-elected, in 2022, he won 63 percent of the vote, easily defeating his progressive challenger.

Sally King, a longtime Plymouth resident who attended Ms. Clancy’s trial, said she would not vote for Mr. Cruz in November. Ms. King, who described herself as a “conservative Democrat” who has supported leaders from both parties, said she would be “infuriated” if the district attorney were to retry Ms. Clancy on the same charges.

“When you have 11 jurors who agreed on insanity?” she said. “There is no justice there.”

item.title: Unruly Passenger Is Restrained With Duct Tape During a Flight
item.description:
An American Airlines flight was traveling as scheduled on Thursday night from Texas to New Jersey when a man suddenly began to shout vulgarities and became violent, according to the authorities and the airline.

That’s when two other passengers, relying on zip ties, duct tape and sheer will, restrained the disruptive man until the authorities could board the plane and take him into custody.

The flight, which was on its way to Newark from Dallas, was diverted to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport.

The Maryland Transportation Authority Police identified the disruptive passenger as Arthur Lundeen, 67.

Maryland court records said Mr. Lundeen, of Tucson, Ariz., waived his right to a lawyer at an initial court appearance on Friday and was released on his own recognizance.

Efforts to reach Mr. Lundeen on Saturday were unsuccessful.

Richard O’Lenick, 53, one of the passengers who restrained Mr. Lundeen, said in a phone interview on Saturday that Mr. Lundeen began to shout racial slurs at one of the flight attendants.

“He was getting very aggressive and very loud,” Mr. O’Lenick said.

Mr. Lundeen then became physical with his seat mate. Mr. Lundeen struck the laptop of the man next to him, and then grabbed the man’s throat, Mr. O’Lenick said. When a woman in a seat ahead of the scuffle tried to intervene, Mr. Lundeen started to attack her as well.

That’s when Mr. O’Lenick and Juan Mejia, a colleague at a New Jersey shooting range, jumped into action from their seats two rows ahead.

Mr. O’Lenick, who tried to keep Mr. Lundeen’s legs down, said Mr. Mejia “proceeds to sit next to the guy to try to control the situation.”

It was not immediately clear what precipitated the violent outburst. A flight attendant rushed over with zip ties but even with his hands restrained, Mr. Lundeen continued to fight.

“I started trying to tell him to relax, we don’t want to hurt you, we just want you to settle down,” Mr. O’Lenick said.

Mr. O’Lenick is the owner and chief financial officer of Gun for Hire, a shooting range and training center in Woodland Park, N.J. Mr. Mejia, who could not be immediately reached on Saturday, is a sales manager at the company and a retired police officer from New Jersey.

The self-defense training both men have practiced was vital for the next 10 minutes, as Mr. Lundeen violently struggled, screamed that the plane was going down and bit Mr. Mejia on his hand, Mr. O’Lenick said.

That’s when a flight attendant brought duct tape, which Mr. Mejia wrapped around Mr. Lundeen’s body and seat, restraining his head as well.

“The entire time the flight attendants were present,” Mr. O’Lenick said. “They were advising throughout the process.”

The plane landed in Baltimore shortly after 10 p.m. where the local authorities boarded the aircraft and removed Mr. Lundeen, who was charged with two misdemeanors, assault in the second degree and disorderly conduct, according to court records.

In a statement, American Airlines confirmed the episode. The Federal Aviation Administration was investigating, the agency said in a statement. The Federal Bureau of Investigation said it was also investigating.

There have been more than 1,160 cases of unruly passengers reported so far this year, according to the F.A.A. That is far fewer than when such episodes peaked in 2021 during the early part of the Covid-19 pandemic, when 5,973 such cases were reported.

In 2021, a passenger on an American Airlines flight who kicked and spat at flight attendants and passengers before attempting to open the cabin door was also restrained with duct tape.

During the scuffle on Thursday’s flight, Mr. Lundeen had somehow cut himself. After the flight landed in Baltimore, a cleaning crew came on board for an hour to sanitize the area, Mr. O’Lenick said.

The Maryland Transportation Authority Police said Mr. Lundeen “was cleared by paramedics for an open wound on his arm.”

Mr. O’Lenick said that once the adrenaline began to fade, he noticed that his pants were covered in blood. He changed into a pair from his luggage. Neither Mr. O’Lenick nor Mr. Mejia sought medical treatment.

After the diverted landing in Baltimore, the flight took off and landed in Newark without incident, Mr. O’Lenick said.

Mr. O’Lenick said that neither he nor Mr. Mejia got complimentary drinks after they restrained Mr. Lundeen, but they did receive much appreciation from their fellow passengers and members of the crew.

That, he said, was enough.

“I feel bad for the guy,” Mr. O’Lenick said. “I don’t know what he was going through. What we do know is that he was getting physical with his actions, and we didn’t know where he was going to stop.”

He added: “We were just there to help.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Robin Morgan, Voice of Radical Feminism, Dies at 85
item.description:
Robin Morgan, a prolific feminist writer and radical activist who edited the landmark 1970 anthology “Sisterhood Is Powerful,” served as editor in chief of Ms. magazine for five years and helped organize one of the first protests of the Miss America pageant, died on Saturday in Manhattan. She was 85.

The death, in a hospital, was confirmed by her son, the musician Blake Morgan, who is her sole survivor.

From the front lines of a much-splintered feminist movement, Ms. Morgan gave voice to women as a poet, journalist, novelist, memoirist, agitator and iconoclast. She came of age in the civil rights and anti-Vietnam War movements, but along with other young women of the new left, she found those movements dominated by men, and, in particular, men who wanted to keep women as second-class citizens.

“We were tired of making coffee and not policy,” she told The Guardian in 2006.

Ms. Morgan caused shock waves in 1970 when she published an essay in Rat, an underground newspaper. The article, titled “Goodbye to All That,” named specific men as sexists. “Goodbye to Hip Culture and the so-called Sexual Revolution,” she wrote, stating that the murderous Charles Manson was “only the logical extreme of the normal American male’s fantasy.” The piece became an instant classic of second-wave feminism; it also brought her death threats from counterculture activists. “They called it ‘the shot heard round the Left,’” she told The New Yorker in 2008.

She returned to that theme in 2008 with “Goodbye to All That (#2),” an essay calling out the toxic misogyny aimed at Hillary Clinton, then a senator who was running for the Democratic presidential nomination. The article went viral (and was mass-forwarded by Chelsea Clinton, her daughter).

Ms. Morgan’s early activism in the late 1960s included cofounding the radical feminist groups Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell and New York Radical Women, which in 1968 organized one of the first protests against the Miss America pageant for its objectification of women.

At the protest, on Atlantic City’s boardwalk in New Jersey, several hundred women staged guerrilla theater actions: Some threw bras, girdles, hair curlers, mops and other symbols of women’s “enslavement” into a trash bin (but, contrary to popular belief, Ms. Morgan insisted that there was no bra burning). The climax of the day’s events was the unfurling of a banner inside the city’s convention hall that said, “Women’s Liberation.” The protest earned Ms. Morgan prominent mention in The New York Times Magazine under the headline, “Meet the Women of the Revolution, 1969.”

She coined the term “herstory” — history written from women’s point of view and claimed partial credit for the slogan “the personal is political.” Her phrase “pornography is the theory; rape is the practice” became a rallying cry for the anti-porn movement.

As the keynote speaker at the 1973 West Coast Lesbian Conference, Ms. Morgan protested the presence of the transgender folk singer Beth Elliott, whose performance became a symbolic dividing line between feminist groups at the event. “No, I will not call a man ‘she,’” Ms. Morgan said in her speech. “Thirty-two years of suffering in this androcentric society, and surviving, have earned me the title of ‘woman.’”

Decades later, this speech earned her the label “trans-exclusionary radical feminist” as 21st-century gender politics brought about a rethinking of sex, gender and transgender rights. When asked about that speech in a 2024 interview for this obituary, she said, “I believe that trans rights are human rights.” Then she paused and sighed before adding, “It’s complicated.”

Ms. Morgan created the iconic image on the cover of “Sisterhood Is Powerful,” taking the symbol for female — a circle above a cross — and filling it with a raised red fist. The book, a comprehensive collection of the writings of second-wave feminists such as Kate Millett, Eleanor Holmes Norton and Florynce Kennedy as well as documents from feminist organizations, became a best seller; it was included in the New York Public Library’s “Books of the Century” exhibition and was named by the American Library Association as one of the 100 most influential books of the 20th century. Ms. Morgan used the royalties to create “The Sisterhood Is Powerful Fund,” a feminist grant-giving organization.

Her second anthology, “Sisterhood Is Global” (1984), focused on interviews with women from around the world, which led her to establish the Sisterhood Is Global Institute with the French activist Simone de Beauvoir. She worked on the book from her office at Ms. magazine, where she was a contributing editor. In 1989, she was asked by its co-founder Gloria Steinem to become editor in chief and re-established the publication as an ad-free, international bimonthly magazine. Circulation soared, and the magazine won numerous journalism awards. She resigned as editor in chief in 1994 but remained on as consulting global editor.

She completed her final “Sisterhood” anthology, “Sisterhood Is Forever,” with essays by more than 50 feminists, in 2003. She then joined forces with Ms. Steinem and Jane Fonda in 2005 to create the Women’s Media Center, a nonprofit organization supporting women working in the media. She hosted a podcast on politics for the center for many years. (Ms. Steinem died on Wednesday.)

By her 80s, Ms. Morgan had published two dozen books, including poetry, novels, nonfiction works and numerous essays in both the mainstream and alternative media. Her books included the best seller, “The Demon Lover: The Roots of Terrorism” (1989), a feminist analysis of violence, and her acclaimed memoir “Saturday’s Child” in 2001.

Robin Evonne Morgan was born on Jan. 29, 1941, in Lake Worth, Fla., to Faith Malkah Teitlebaum Berkley, a sales clerk at Lerner Stores, a women’s clothing chain. Faith was not married and had traveled to Florida from New York to hide her pregnancy; for years, she told Robin that she was born in 1942.

Robin did not meet her father, Dr. Mordechai Morgenstern, a gynecologist, until she was 20. He handed her a birth certificate that revealed she had been born a year earlier.

Robin’s aunt pushed her into child modeling and Faith became an aggressive stage mother. By age 5, Robin had her own half-hour weekly call-in radio program, “The Little Robin Morgan Show,” on WOR in New York. At around age 8, she began appearing on TV and starred in the popular show “Mama,” about a working-class Norwegian immigrant family in turn-of-the-century San Francisco. When she was a teenager, she quit acting to become a writer against her mother’s wishes. She enrolled in nonmatriculated literature classes at Columbia University at 16.

Instead of earning a degree, she landed a secretarial job with the Curtis Brown literary agency by her early 20s, which gave her access to influential writers such as W.H. Auden. She joined a writing workshop, where she met the poet Kenneth Pitchford, a founder of the Gay Liberation Front. They married in 1962, shortly after his boyfriend broke up with him — and served as best man at their wedding.

As an adult, she loathed any mention of her having been a child star. She famously walked off “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson,” which was airing live, in 1969, when it showed footage of her as a child actor while she was talking to Mr. Carson about rape. “Imagine talking about such a subject and having it trivialized like that,” she told The Guardian.

Her marriage ended in divorce in 1990. Mr. Pitchford died in 2020.

She always remained prolific — and fiery.

“I’m now 77,” she said in 2018, “which once would have sounded positively antique to me. But I just came out with my 23rd book.” She added: “I am still intensely an activist. When younger women come to me for advice, I smile. ‘Get your own torch,’ I tell them, ‘I’m not done with mine yet.’”

item.title: A Sympathetic Plaintiff and Well-Crafted Defense Dominated Clancy Trial
item.description:
Kevin Reddington, a veteran trial lawyer, kicked off the defense of his client earlier this summer with an audacious assertion, given that his client is Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts nurse who had admitted to strangling her three young children.

“This,” Mr. Reddington told 12 jurors in his opening remarks, “is not a righteous prosecution.”

Eleven of those jurors voted not to convict Ms. Clancy, 36, who claimed she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. With one holdout juror, the judge declared a mistrial, leaving a question mark hovering over a murder case that set off a global conversation about the mental health burdens of motherhood, and long-held questions about the essential fairness of the insanity defense.

A retrial is possible. But for now, the mistrial must be considered a victory for Mr. Reddington, one that allows his client to return, for the time being at least, to a state-run psychiatric hospital rather than a prison cell.

But if Mr. Reddington is to be believed, it will not register as a win for Ms. Clancy. During the trial, he described her as a mother well aware of what she had done to her children and “living her own hell.”

Such statements by Mr. Reddington were part of a defense strategy that acknowledged Ms. Clancy’s dark actions but emphasized her mental health problems and the missteps of the medical establishment as she sought help. In the wake of the six-week trial, a number of legal experts said that Mr. Reddington, 75, had masterfully pulled off an astonishingly difficult courtroom assignment amid the most macabre of circumstances.

The jurors were forced to consider the horrors, not only of the killing, but also of Ms. Clancy’s attempted suicide, in detail so gruesome that Mr. Reddington apologized to them. “God bless you,” he said. “You people are going to have to listen to some of the most horrific things, look at some of the most horrific things.”

Trying to convince jurors to consider an insanity defense is not easy in such circumstances.

“There’s something in human nature that makes people want to assign blame,” said Shira M. Diner, who teaches at Boston University Law School. There is a desire to mete out a punishment that “can make people feel, not better, but feel more at peace with the horrors that they learned about” she said.

Even so, Mr. Reddington had an important factor that worked in his favor. Under Massachusetts law, it is up to prosecutors to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a defendant like Ms. Clancy, who claims to be suffering from mental illness, was “criminally responsible” for her conduct at the time of killing — meaning that the defendant lacked “the substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality or wrongfulness of his conduct or to conform his conduct to the requirements of the law.”

R. Michael Cassidy, a professor at Boston College Law School, said that Massachusetts “is one of a handful of states where, once the defense of ‘lack of criminal responsibility’ is raised, the burden is on the government to disprove it beyond a reasonable doubt. That’s not true in many states, and it’s not true in federal court. The defendant must prove lack of criminal responsibility by a preponderance of the evidence in most states, and in federal court, they have to prove it by clear and convincing evidence.”

Mr. Reddington sought to instill a sense of doubt in the jurors from the outset.

“The government says that this is a situation that’s not a referendum on women’s having babies and having postpartum psychosis, postpartum depression, but it sure as hell is,” he told the jury.

The strong language was a good introduction to jurors of Mr. Reddington’s style. He wore a dark suit on the first day of the trial, a likely acknowledgment of the gravity of the situation. But his language could be down-to-earth and occasionally salty — unsurprising for a man who has tried high-profile cases for decades but rides a Harley in his spare time.

He was also focused on hammering home the message that jurors should reject the prosecution’s argument that Ms. Clancy had acted “rationally” in carrying out the killings.

“What I think Reddington did early on is he made this a reasonable doubt case,” said Daniel S. Medwed, a professor at Northeastern University School of Law in Boston. “We don’t know exactly, of course, what happened in the deliberation room, but at least some of the reporting and some of the revelations in court indicated that the jurors were focused on reasonable doubt.”

Mr. Medwed said that Mr. Reddington may have helped win over jurors with the empathy he showed toward his client. For much of the trial, she sat next to him at the defense table in a wheelchair; Mr. Reddington explained to jurors that she was paralyzed from the waist down, the result of a jump from a second-story window after she had killed her children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023. She had cut her wrists and neck before she had jumped.

Over the course of the trial, Mr. Reddington described his client as a woman who had been a professional caregiver, friend and mother until she began suffering from extreme mental anguish and seeking out solutions in vain. But because Ms. Clancy did not take the stand, the portrait was only Mr. Reddington’s to paint. Mr. Medwed said he had done so deftly.

“It seemed like he had a genuine empathy for her, and I think that matters,” he said. “That matters in any case. But I think it really matters in a case where the defendant refrains from testifying.”

Prosecutors portrayed Ms. Clancy as manipulative and deliberate in her actions, arguing that she sent her husband out on errands to give her time to kill the children. The claims of postpartum psychosis, they argued, were efforts to evade responsibility for her actions.

To Joe Serpa, a Massachusetts defense lawyer, this amounted to a “cruel and tone-deaf posture” by the state.

“Lindsay Clancy is an obviously sympathetic defendant,” Mr. Serpa wrote on his legal blog. “She lost all three of her children. She attempted to die by suicide and survived. Her mental illness was documented before the killings by the medications she had been prescribed and the treatment she had sought. She has been left paralyzed.”

He added: “Against those facts, telling a jury that this woman coldly wanted her own children dead asks it to accept something that does not correspond to what it can see.”

But for Timothy Cruz, the Plymouth County district attorney, the decision to try Ms. Clancy on three first-degree murder charges, which would have resulted in life in prison without parole, was “about getting justice for those three little babies.”

After the mistrial was declared on Friday, Mr. Cruz said he had not yet made a decision about whether to retry the case.

A plea agreement is one possibility. But if Mr. Cruz decides on a retrial, it could take on a number of forms. Mr. Cassidy said that prosecutors could seek a lesser charge, like second-degree murder or manslaughter. They could also seek a bench trial, in which the judge, rather than a jury, could decide Ms. Clancy’s fate.

Mr. Cassidy said that if Mr. Reddington were to return to the courtroom, he might try to have some of the most horrific evidence entered into the record based on the transcripts of previous testimony, rather than a live rehashing by witnesses on the stand.

Prosecutors could object, and seek to revisit these stories with live witnesses, but they will most likely have to weigh some practical considerations.

“I mean, this trial took six weeks,” Mr. Cassidy said. “That’s a lot of court resources and Plymouth County D.A. resources.”

But Mr. Cassidy said that at this point, many observers may have come to consider the matter as “a classic instance of insanity” unworthy of a retrial.

“I mean, if this isn’t insanity,” he said, “what is?”
